This is a new mechanic, so here are my questions before I write any code. Each has a suggested default; reply "defaults" or change any of them. So far I've only pushed this turn's AI log, in PR #46: https://github.com/fischerq/ludumdare60/pull/46. Plan usage: 5-hour 5 %, weekly 19 %.

1. **Which layers?** I'm reading "lower levels" as the seven deep layers (-1 screen down to -7 input wires).
   *Default: only those seven. The maze, cabinet and hall stay as they are.*

2. **Tron look, but still pixel art?** The master doc says pixel art throughout, at whole zoom factors.
   *Default: yes. Thin neon lines with a 1–2 px glow drawn into the pixels, a faint grid floor, no blur shaders. Each layer gets a very dark background color and one neon accent.*

3. **Colors per layer.** *Default, going down:*
   - -1 screen: magenta on a near-black plum
   - -2 signals: cyan on a dark teal
   - -3 video memory: blue on indigo
   - -4 bus: amber on a dark brown
   - -5 CPU: green on a dark green
   - -6 logic: violet on a dark purple
   - -7 wires: orange on a dark rust

   Every layer also uses white, and one shared red for hazards.

4. **How does the player move?** The swipe-one-tile grid walker goes away.
   - (a) Free movement: drag and Pac-Man moves toward your finger, like the movement lab bench. Each layer's topology shapes the walls and obstacles.
   - (b) Rails: you move along the layer's own lines (bus lanes, circuit traces, graph edges) and switch at junctions.

   *Default: (a) in most layers, (b) only where the topology really is lines (bus, wires).*

5. **One area per layer: does this fit?** *Default:*
   - -1 screen: the tall picture tube with rounded corners and vertical scanline stripes
   - -2 signals: a corridor that splits tile → palette → output, flowing down the screen
   - -3 video memory: stacked memory banks (rows of bytes with gaps between them)
   - -4 bus: 24 parallel lanes, highway-style
   - -5 CPU: the listing as a tall scrolling tower, with registers as side rooms
   - -6 logic: a node graph (junctions and paths, no walls)
   - -7 wires: a circuit board with traces between the switch pads

   The hazards from today's version stay.

6. **Tron mechanics, or only the look?** For example, a light-cycle trail behind Pac-Man that turns into a wall or hazard.
   *Default: look only. The trail is a harmless glowing streak that fades.*

7. **What about dots and Pac-Man?** Today each layer collects different things: hex codes, bits, Z/C flags.
   *Default: every collectible is a round Pac dot in the layer's accent color, with a tiny label (bit, flag, byte) where it helps. Pac-Man is a neon outline in that color. Following Max's rules, that means one folder per layer (`assets/deep/<layer>/`) with the colors drawn in, 32x32, no tinting.*

8. **Order and size.** *Default:*
   - First, one commit that applies the style to all seven layers (colors, neon look, dots, Pac-Man). You can playtest that on its own.
   - Then the new areas, one layer per commit, starting with the bus (-4), because lanes are the clearest case.

   Rebuilding all seven areas is a big job. I'll check usage before each layer.

I've restyled all seven deep layers in a Tron look and replaced the maze walls with open areas in four of them; it's pushed to PR #46: https://github.com/fischerq/ludumdare60/pull/46. I checked every layer in a headless phone-size browser: no console errors, and screenshots of two layers are saved for the making-of.

**The look**
- **Colors per layer:** each layer has its own dark background, which fills the whole screen behind it, plus one neon accent. Going down: magenta, cyan, blue, amber, green, violet, orange.
- **Shared colors:** everything deadly is the same red in every layer, and white is used everywhere.
- **Style:** still pixel art, with a faint floor grid, neon lines with a 1 px glow, and a neon edge around the play area.
- **Dots:** every collectible is now a dot in the layer's accent colors. Only the power pellets get more detail (a ring with a core).

- **Art files:** the dots, special dots and Pac-Man frames are in `assets/deep/<layer>/`, so Max can redraw them. The grids, walls and lanes are still drawn in code each frame.

**The areas**
Movement is still one tile per swipe. Four layers no longer use the maze walls to block you:
- **Screen (-1):** you can walk the whole tube except its rounded corners. The maze walls now count as lit, so the beam kills you on a wall just like on an uneaten dot. That makes this layer harder; stay in the dark gaps when the beam comes.
- **Signals (-2), video RAM (-3) and logic (-6):** the whole grid is open. The walls are drawn dimly so they read as data on the floor.
- **Bus, CPU and wires:** these already had their own layouts and only got restyled.

These open areas are a first pass. With no walls, those four layers now differ mostly in their hazards and look rather than in their shape, so each one may still need a real layout of its own.

turns.reply:
The merge conflicts on PR #46 are fixed: the branch now contains the latest `main`, which brought in PR #48. https://github.com/fischerq/ludumdare60/pull/46

The cause was a gap in the setup. The turn-start hook did merge `main`, but only on the local copy, and nothing pushed that merge until the end of a turn. So GitHub showed the PR in conflict while the fix sat unpushed. And when `main` moved while no session was running, nothing reacted at all.

**What I changed:**
- **The turn-start merge is pushed right away.** After a clean merge, `tools/sync_main.py` now pushes immediately, as long as the branch is already on GitHub. The PR comes out of conflict at the start of the turn instead of the end.
- **New GitHub Action, `.github/workflows/sync-prs.yml`.** On every push to `main`, it merges `main` into each open PR branch from this repo, using the same script. The generated making-of files are rebuilt, so they never block a merge. If a real conflict remains, it leaves the branch untouched and posts one comment on the PR; the next session on that branch resolves it as before.
- **`CLAUDE.md`** explains both.

I tested the script's clean-merge and real-conflict paths on a throwaway copy of the repo. The clean merge went through and the conflict case left no half-done merge behind. The Action itself hasn't run yet; its first run will be on the next push to `main`, after this PR is merged. If it fails then, the likely cause is that GitHub Actions isn't allowed to push in the repo settings ("Workflow permissions" needs to be "Read and write").

Plan usage: 5-hour 6 %, weekly 19 %.

**To test on the phone:** nothing changed in the game, but the deep layers from the last turn are now up to date with `main`, so you can playtest them from the PR's preview.

I've written a research survey and one gameplay proposal per layer into `design/systems/topdown-mechanics.md`; nothing is built yet. Below are the questions to answer before I build. PR: https://github.com/fischerq/ludumdare60/pull/49

**Research.** The survey is a table of room mechanics from Zelda, Pokémon and grid puzzle games, each matched to something in the machine:

| Mechanic | Where it's from | Machine match |
|---|---|---|
| Dark rooms | Zelda, Pokémon Flash caves | The picture tube |
| Ice sliding | Pokémon Ice Path | A signal running down a wire |
| Spinner tiles and conveyors | Pokémon Rocket Hideout, Mossdeep Gym; Zelda | Data being carried |
| Warp panels | Pokémon Saffron Gym | `JP`/`CALL` |
| Crystal-switch blocks | Zelda | CPU flags |
| Pressure plates and push blocks | Zelda, Sokoban | Joystick switches, moving bytes |
| Trainer line of sight | Pokémon | Ghost target vectors |
| Beamos and blade traps | Zelda | Program counter, write head |
| Beat-locked enemies | Crypt of the NecroDancer | The vblank tick |

The doc ends with one proposal per layer, each with its own verb, and the beam sweep only on the screen.

**Also fixed.** PR #46 was merged in the meantime. The turn-start hook I added last turn then pushed a merge onto that already-merged branch, leaving pushed commits no open PR covered. It now skips the push in that case. I restarted the branch from `main`, and the new PR is #49.

**Questions** (defaults in italics; reply "defaults" or change any):

1. **Which layers change, and in what order?** *Default: all seven get their own mechanic, one commit per layer so you can playtest each. Order: signals (-2), CPU (-5), logic (-6), video RAM (-3), bus (-4), wires (-7), screen (-1, which mostly stays).*
2. **-2 Signals: carry and deliver.** The row sweep goes. You pick up a color index at a dot tile; it trails behind you like a Pokémon follower. You carry it to the palette chip, then to the DAC at the screen edge, and only delivered colors count. *Default: yes. One color at a time. A sprite hitting you drops it.*
3. **Sound waves on -2.** The rising wave at the bottom is close to a sweep. *Default: replace it with a timed trap. Each sound command makes the sound chip's tiles pulse deadly for a moment, NecroDancer-style.*
4. **-5 CPU: warps plus switch blocks.**
   - Stepping on a `CALL`/`JP` line warps you to its target line; `RET` takes you back.
   - Z and C flags raise and lower two colors of blocks across the listing, like Zelda's crystal switches.
   - The program counter is a Beamos-like hazard.
   - The goal becomes collecting flags or visiting routines.

   *Default: all four.*
5. **-6 Logic: line of sight instead of instant death.** Crossing a ghost's target vector gets you spotted ("!"), and that ghost chases you on the grid for a few seconds. A frightened ghost can't see, so eating its pellet node makes you safe for a while. *Default: yes; being caught counts as a hit.*
6. **-3 Video RAM: blade trap.** The read sweep goes. The CPU's write head waits at the row's edge, then dashes along the row to the address it writes. *Default: blade trap yes. Push blocks (pushing a byte onto a target address) not now.*
7. **-4 Bus: should the scrolling stay?** The scrolling rows are sweep-like too.
   - (a) Keep the scrolling timeline, but make 1-lanes spinner tiles that carry you down, so 1s push you instead of killing you.
   - (b) Rebuild it as a spatial bus: CPU on one side, chips as rooms, the address decoder opening one chip's door at a time.

   *Default: (a) now, since it's smaller; (b) later if wanted.*
8. **-7 Wires: add a push block?** A push block you can shove onto a switch pad would hold a direction while you walk to another pad. *Default: yes, one block. The screen layer (-1) stays as it is, with the beam as the only sweep.*

| -3 Video RAM | Blade trap: the write head waits at the start of its row, then dashes to its address | The write head | The 4 power-pellet bytes |

| -6 Logic | Crossing a ghost's target line gets you spotted | A seeker that hunts you for 6 s | Stand on each ghost's target tile |
| -7 Wires | Switch pads, plus a block you push onto a pad to hold it | A noise spark crawling after you; Pac-Man dying | Steer Pac-Man into all 4 maze corners |

- **Logic:** only Blinky has a target at first; the other three appear once they leave the ghost house.
